overview.text: Sharks are a diverse group of cartilaginous fishes in class Chondrichthyes, related to rays and skates; the great white, also called the white shark, is just one species. Their skeletons are made mainly of cartilage rather than bone, and most sharks have five separate gill slits on each side (some have six or seven). Many have several rows of teeth that are continually replaced. Their senses include a lateral line that detects water movement and ampullae of Lorenzini—sensory pores that detect weak electric fields, useful for finding concealed prey. Many sharks are predators that help shape marine food webs, but shark species differ greatly in size, diet, habitat, and behavior.

key_facts.text: Sharks, rays, and chimaeras belong to the cartilaginous-fish class Chondrichthyes; a shark’s skeleton is made mainly of cartilage.
Most sharks have five gill slits on each side of the head, while some species have six or seven.
Sharks continually shed and replace teeth; tooth shapes vary with what different species eat.
The lateral line senses water movement, while ampullae of Lorenzini detect weak electric fields that can help sharks find hidden prey.
Shark skin is covered in tiny scales called dermal denticles, which reduce drag as the shark moves through water.
Sharks are predators that can help keep prey populations in check, contributing to the ecological balance of their environments.
